The oft-quoted portion of the Windows 10 TOS that has the infamous "we will share your data" bit is being widely misread here. That portion repeatedly refers to Microsoft "services".

Disclaimer: I'm not addressing the telemetry or local search issues here. This is a very specific claim I'm addressing which I've seen repeated ad nauseam - "Windows 10 sends the contents of your hard drive to Microsoft."

First you have to understand that in tech, "service" means something specific, that is, something hosted on a server. To demonstrate, check out how the tech world uses the term "service":

Desktop as a Service (DaaS) is a cloud service in which the back-end of a virtual desktop infrastructure (VDI) is hosted by a cloud service provider.

http://searchvirtualdesktop.techtarget.com/definition/desktop-as-a-service-DaaS

Software as a Service (SaaS) is a software distribution model in which applications are hosted by a vendor or service provider and made available to customers over a network, typically the Internet.

http://searchcloudcomputing.techtarget.com/definition/Software-as-a-Service

Your hard drive in your Windows computer is not a service. OneDrive, Outlook.com, and Cortana, are. Any program you use, which is running on a computer in "the cloud" could be called a service. Your personal PC, unless it is itself offerring "services" to another PC (which would make it, unsurprisingly, a "server") is not a service. It is not what this portion of the TOS is referring to whatsoever.

This portion of the TOS alone makes no indication whatsoever that Microsoft is reporting to anyone, including themselves, about your personal files, unless you happen to place those personal files into one of their online services.

The sticky part is that while some of these "services" are not switched on by default, some are. That is indeed Microsoft's fault, and users interested in maintaining a high degree of privacy on their devices should be aware of that.

However, in case you're thinking those terms are some kind of draconian new development, check out the privacy policy for some other service providers. Note that I'm only copying the portion regarding law enforcement, as the rest of their data gathering is extremely similar as well, though this portion seems to be the hot button issue:

Gmail:

We will share personal information with companies, organizations or individuals outside of Google if we have a good-faith belief that access, use, preservation or disclosure of the information is reasonably necessary to: - meet any applicable law, regulation, legal process or enforceable governmental request. - enforce applicable Terms of Service, including investigation of potential violations. - detect, prevent, or otherwise address fraud, security or technical issues. - protect against harm to the rights, property or safety of Google, our users or the public as required or permitted by law.

Yahoo:

We respond to subpoenas, court orders, or legal process (such as law enforcement requests), or to establish or exerJewe our legal rights or defend against legal claims. We believe it is necessary to share information in order to investigate, prevent, or take action regarding illegal activities, suspected fraud, situations involving potential threats to the physical safety of any person, violations of Yahoo's terms of use, or as otherwise required by law.

Dropbox:

Law & Order. We may disclose your information to third parties if we determine that such disclosure is reasonably necessary to (a) comply with the law; (b) protect any person from death or serious bodily injury; (c) prevent fraud or abuse of Dropbox or our users; or (d) protect Dropbox's property rights.

TL;DR: Attempting to understand this situation without the appropriate knowledge of terms can lead to some pretty amazing interpretations.
